question: "Upon this rock." What is revelation, really?
intro: Peter said Jesus was the Christ, and Jesus said flesh and blood didn't tell him that. The Father did. Then He said He'd build His Church on "this rock." Catholics say the rock is Peter. We say the rock is revelation. Either way, Jesus is saying the whole thing runs on God actually talking to people. So what does that look like, and how do you know when it's Him?

days.q: What did Peter say, and what did Jesus say back?
days.intro: Read the conversation at Caesarea Philippi. Jesus asks two questions. The first is easy. The second is the only one that matters. When you read, notice where Jesus says Peter's answer came from.
days.journal: "Whom say ye that I am?" Answer it yourself, right now, in one sentence. Then write where that answer came from.

days.q: Why there, and what's the rock?
days.intro: Caesarea Philippi sat at the base of a massive rock cliff with a cave in it that pagans called the gate of hell. There was a temple to Caesar built into it. Jesus took His disciples to the most pagan spot in the region and asked who He was. Then He said the gates of hell wouldn't prevail against His Church, with the actual gate of hell in view. The Greek: Peter is *petros*, a stone. "This rock" is *petra*, bedrock. He's not building on a pebble.
days.journal: Helaman says build on the rock of the Redeemer so the devil's storms can't drag you down. What are you actually built on? Be specific.

days.q: How does the Restoration describe revelation?
days.intro: The D&C has more detail about how revelation works than the rest of scripture combined. Read the Lord explaining it to Oliver Cowdery, twice, because Oliver didn't get it the first time. Then read Alma asking how *he* knows. When you read, list every method you find.
days.journal: D&C 8 says it comes to your mind and your heart. Which one do you trust more? Which one do you ignore?

days.q: What does the prophet say about revelation?
days.intro: President Russell M. Nelson, April 2018. His first conference as prophet, and he used it to tell everyone that personal revelation is the whole game.

read.talk: Revelation for the Church, Revelation for Our Lives
read.speaker: Russell M. Nelson

days.takeaway: His point is that in the coming days it won't be possible to survive spiritually without the guiding influence of the Holy Ghost. Not "it'll be nice." Not possible. He describes how he gets revelation: write down the question, study it out, pray, write down the impressions, and act. And he says you can get better at it, the way you get better at anything, by doing it a lot.
days.journal: Nelson describes a process: ask, study, write, act. Which step do you skip?

days.q: How do you know it's God and not just you?
days.intro: Here's the hard part, and it's the real question. You get a feeling. Is that the Spirit or is that you wanting something? Joseph Smith learned this the hard way. He kept asking the Lord if Martin Harris could take the manuscript until he got the answer he wanted, and the 116 pages were gone. Read what the Lord told him afterward, and look for how He tells you to test it next time.
days.journal: Think of a time you were sure something was revelation and it wasn't. What does that teach you about the times you're sure now?

days.q: How do you get more of it?
days.intro: Nephi gives you the how in one verse: he *desired* to know, he *believed* it was possible, and he *sat pondering*. That's it. Then read D&C 88, which tells you to draw near and promises He'll draw near back. Then the Lord's instruction about pondering things out. When you read, look for what you're supposed to do before the revelation comes.
read: Preach My Gospel, chapter 4, "Recognize the Spirit"
days.journal: Pick one question you actually want an answer to. Write it down. Then do Nelson's process this week and come back to it on Day 7.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to Caesarea Philippi. Read Peter's confession one more time. Then read the question you wrote on Day 6, and what you wrote on Day 1.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: What is revelation, really? And did you get any this week?

question: How many times do I really have to forgive someone who keeps doing it?
intro: Peter thought he was being generous when he asked about seven times. Jesus said seventy times seven, and then told a story about a guy who was forgiven a fortune and then choked somebody over pocket change. Everybody knows we're supposed to forgive. Almost nobody knows what to do with the person who never stops, or never says sorry, or actually hurt you badly. This week is about that person.

days.q: What did Jesus say, and what story did He tell?
days.intro: Read Peter's question and the parable that follows. Notice the amounts. Ten thousand talents was more money than existed in the whole region. A hundred pence was a few months' wages. Jesus picked those numbers on purpose. When you read, figure out who you are in the story. The answer is uncomfortable.
days.journal: Who's the person you've forgiven the most times? Who's the person you haven't forgiven once? Write both names.

days.q: Where did "seventy times seven" come from?
days.intro: Here's something almost nobody catches. In Genesis 4, a man named Lamech brags that if Cain was avenged seven times, he'll be avenged seventy-seven times. It's the first recorded escalation of revenge in scripture. Jesus takes Lamech's number and flips it from vengeance to forgiveness. He's not giving Peter a quota. He's undoing a curse. Read Lamech first, then Jesus again.
days.journal: Lamech's math was "you hurt me once, I hurt you seventy-seven times." Where are you keeping that kind of math on someone?

days.q: What does the Restoration require?
days.intro: D&C 64 has the sentence that settles it, and it's harder than the New Testament. "Of you it is required to forgive all men." Not encouraged. Required. Read it, then read what the Lord told Alma about members who won't forgive each other. When you read, notice who the Lord says the unforgiving person is actually hurting.
days.journal: D&C 64:9 says the one who won't forgive has the greater sin. Does that feel fair? Why does the Lord say it anyway?

days.q: What do apostles say about forgiving?
days.intro: Elder Jeffrey R. Holland, April 2018. He talks about forgiveness in families, in the Church, and with yourself, and he doesn't pretend it's easy.
days.takeaway: His point is that holding a grudge is like drinking poison and waiting for the other person to die. He says forgiveness is a gift you give yourself as much as them, and that carrying the wound around doesn't hurt the person who caused it. He also says something important: forgiving isn't the same as saying it didn't matter. It mattered. You forgive anyway.
days.journal: Holland says the grudge hurts you, not them. What's the grudge that's been costing you the most?

days.q: Does forgiving mean trusting them again?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. Someone hurt you badly. Maybe they're not sorry. Maybe they'll do it again. Does forgiving mean letting them back in? No. Forgiveness and trust are different things. Read D&C 98, which is the Lord's actual instruction about people who keep coming back to hurt you. It's more nuanced than people think. Then read Jesus on enemies. Figure out what forgiveness requires and what it doesn't.
days.journal: Who do you need to forgive but not trust? What would forgiving them look like if it doesn't mean letting them close?

days.q: How do you actually do it?
days.intro: Jesus gives one instruction that works: pray for them. Not pray that they change. Pray *for* them. It's almost impossible to keep hating someone you're sincerely praying for. Then read Nephi, who was hunted by his own brothers and still calls his heart's anger a weakness he needs to fix. Then read Joseph, who forgave the brothers who sold him, and had to tell them again seventeen years later because they still didn't believe it. When you read, look for what forgiveness does to the forgiver.
days.journal: Take the name from Day 1 that you haven't forgiven. Pray for them tonight, by name, for good things. Then write one sentence about what it was like.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to the parable. Read it once more and find the moment the servant could have chosen differently. Then read your Day 1 answer.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: How many times do you really have to forgive? And what about the person who isn't sorry?

question: Who is my neighbor, and why did Jesus make the hero a Samaritan?
intro: A lawyer asked Jesus "who is my neighbor?" trying to find the edge of the rule. Who do I *have* to love, so I know who I don't. Jesus told a story where the priest and the Levite, the religious guys, walk past, and a Samaritan, the guy every Jew hated, stops. That wasn't a nice story to them. It was offensive. This week is about why.

days.q: What was the question, and what was the story?
days.intro: Read the whole exchange. Notice the lawyer's second question comes because he wanted to "justify himself." Notice that Jesus never answers "who is my neighbor." He flips it to "who *was* a neighbor." Different question. When you read, count how many people walked past.
days.journal: The lawyer wanted to know the minimum. Who's outside your circle right now, the people you've decided you don't have to care about?

days.q: Why a Samaritan?
days.intro: Samaritans were half-Israelites left over from the Assyrian conquest, mixed with foreigners, with their own temple on the wrong mountain. Jews and Samaritans hated each other for centuries. Jews would walk days out of their way to avoid Samaria. And here's the kicker: just one chapter earlier in Luke, James and John asked Jesus if they could call down fire on a Samaritan village. Read that first. Then read the woman at the well being shocked He'd even talk to her.
days.journal: James and John wanted to burn a Samaritan village. A week later Jesus made a Samaritan the hero. Who's the group you'd have a hard time hearing praised?

days.q: What does King Benjamin say about who deserves help?
days.intro: King Benjamin takes the excuse away before you can make it. The beggar brought it on himself? Doesn't matter. Read his logic. Then read the line about serving people being the same as serving God. When you read, look for how he answers the objection "but they don't deserve it."
days.journal: King Benjamin says we're all beggars. What have you received that you didn't deserve?

days.q: What do apostles say about being the neighbor?
days.intro: President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, April 2010. He tells a story about a statue of Christ with no hands, and what somebody wrote on the sign.
days.takeaway: His point is that Christ's love for people gets delivered through *us*, or it doesn't get delivered. He says we're His hands. He also says something that stings: we sometimes treat people badly and think it's fine because they're not in our ward or our group. The Samaritan didn't check the guy's tribe before he stopped.
days.journal: Uchtdorf says you're His hands. Whose hands were you this week? Whose weren't you?

days.q: The priest and the Levite had reasons. What are yours?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. The priest and Levite weren't villains. Touching a dead body made you unclean for a week and they had temple duties. The road was dangerous and it could've been a trap. They had *reasons*. Good ones. So do you. Read these and then be honest about which of your reasons the Lord would accept.
days.journal: Think of the last time you walked past someone who needed help. What was your reason? Would it hold up in Matthew 25?

days.q: How do you become the Samaritan?
days.intro: The Samaritan did specific things. He saw, he went to him, he bandaged, he carried, he paid, he came back. Six verbs. Then read Matthew 25, where Jesus tells you exactly what counts, and D&C 81, where the Lord tells you what to do with hanging hands. When you read, look for the verbs and pick one.
days.journal: Pick one person outside your normal circle. Do one of the Samaritan's six verbs for them this week. Write down who and which one.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to the story. Read it once more. Then read your Day 1 answer.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: Who is your neighbor? And why did Jesus pick a Samaritan?

question: Why is the older brother in the prodigal son story?
intro: Everybody knows the prodigal son. Kid takes his inheritance, blows it, comes home, dad runs to him. It's the greatest repentance story ever told. But the story doesn't end there. There's an older brother who did everything right and is furious. Jesus put him in on purpose. He was talking to Pharisees who were mad He ate with sinners. This week is about the brother nobody talks about, and why you might be him.

days.q: What does the story say, all of it?
days.intro: Read the whole parable, but pay special attention to the last eight verses. The story doesn't end with the party. It ends with the older brother outside, refusing to come in, and the father going out to *him* too. When you read, notice how the father treats both sons.
days.journal: Which brother are you most like right now? Not which one you want to be. Which one you are.

days.q: How offensive was this to the people listening?
days.intro: In that culture, asking for your inheritance early was wishing your father dead. The father running was undignified; old men didn't run. And the older brother refusing to come to the feast was a public insult to his father in front of the whole village. Every person listening would have been shocked at all three. Then read who Jesus was actually talking to. That's the point of the whole chapter.
read: Luke 15:3-10 (the two stories He told first)
days.journal: The older brother's complaint is "I never did anything wrong and I never got a party." When have you felt that about someone else's forgiveness?

days.q: Who else got angry at God's mercy?
days.intro: Jonah. He preached to Nineveh, they repented, God spared them, and Jonah was furious. He literally asked God to kill him because God was too merciful. Read that. Then read Alma the Elder reacting when his rebellious son came home. One father was angry at mercy. The other rejoiced. When you read, look at what each one wanted.
days.journal: God asks Jonah "doest thou well to be angry?" Where are you angry that God is merciful to someone?

days.q: What does an apostle say about the older brother?
days.intro: Elder Jeffrey R. Holland, April 2002. He gave a whole talk on the older brother. It's called "The Other Prodigal" and the title is the point.
days.takeaway: His point is that the older brother was also lost, just not in a far country. He was lost at home, in resentment and comparison, keeping score. Holland says the father's line to him is the key: "thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine." The older brother already had everything and couldn't see it because he was looking at what his brother got.
days.journal: Holland says the older brother was lost in comparison. Who do you compare yourself to that makes you miss what you already have?

days.q: Isn't the older brother right?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. His complaint is legitimate. He did stay. He did work. He never got the party. If you've been the faithful one while somebody else got the attention for coming back, you know exactly how he felt. So is grace unfair? Read the laborers again from Week 12. Then read Luke 15:7, which Jesus said before the story, and figure out what heaven thinks the party is for.
days.journal: Is grace unfair? Write your honest answer, then write what you'd lose if God were fair by your math.

days.q: How do you stop keeping score?
days.intro: Repentance week (Week 11) was about turning. This is the other half: how you treat people who are turning. Read your Week 11 Day 7 answer first, where you rewrote "repent" in your own words. Then read how the Lord wants us to feel when somebody repents. When you read, look for the word "joy."
days.journal: Think of someone who came back to church, or is trying to. Did you rejoice, or did you keep score? What would rejoicing actually look like this week?

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to the father going out to the older son. Read those verses one more time. Then read your Day 1 answer.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: Why is the older brother in the story? And did you change your answer about which one you are?

question: "What lack I yet?" What would Jesus tell you to sell?
intro: A rich young man kept every commandment and still felt like something was missing. He asked Jesus what. Jesus told him, and it was the one thing he wouldn't give up. He walked away sad. The question isn't whether he was a bad guy. He wasn't. The question is what Jesus would say to *you* if you asked, and whether you'd actually ask.

days.q: What did he ask, and what did Jesus say?
days.intro: Read Matthew's account. Then read Mark's, which has one detail that changes the whole story: before Jesus answered, He looked at the man and loved him. This wasn't a rebuke. It was an invitation from someone who wanted him. When you read, notice that the man was actually good.
days.journal: If you asked Jesus "what lack I yet" and He actually answered, what do you think He'd say? Write your guess.

days.q: Why was everyone shocked?
days.intro: In that world, wealth meant God's favor. If you were rich you were obviously righteous. So when Jesus said it's hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom, the disciples were floored. If *he* can't get in, who can? Read their reaction and Jesus's answer. Then read what He'd said about treasure earlier.
days.journal: The disciples assumed rich meant righteous. What do you assume means righteous? Success? Church calling? A good marriage?

days.q: What does the Book of Mormon say about riches?
days.intro: Jacob, Nephi's brother, doesn't say money is evil. He says the *order* matters. Seek the kingdom first, then riches if you want, and only to do good. King Benjamin adds the rule. Alma shows the church getting it right for a while. When you read, look for the order and the purpose.
days.journal: Jacob says seek the kingdom *first*. What are you actually seeking first, if you judge by your calendar and your bank account?

days.q: What does a modern leader say about the question?
days.intro: Elder Larry R. Lawrence, October 2015. He built a whole talk on this one question and told stories of people who actually asked it.
days.takeaway: His point is that the question works. People who sincerely ask the Lord "what lack I yet" get an answer, and it's usually specific and small, not "sell everything." A sister was told to stop complaining. A brother was told to get to church on time. He says the Spirit can tell you exactly what's next if you ask and mean it.
days.journal: Lawrence says the answers are usually small and specific. Ask tonight. Write down whatever comes, even if it seems dumb.

days.q: Does Jesus want everyone to sell everything?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. He told this guy to sell it all. Did He mean that for everyone? The early Saints in Acts actually did it, and then Ananias lied about it and dropped dead. The Lord gave Joseph Smith the law of consecration and most of the Saints couldn't live it. So what's the actual standard? Read these and figure out whether Jesus is asking for your stuff or something else.
days.journal: Is the standard "give everything" or "be willing to give everything"? What's the difference in practice for you?

days.q: What are you actually holding onto?
days.intro: The rich young man's thing was money. Yours might not be. It might be a grudge, a habit, an identity, a plan, or your comfort. The test is what you'd walk away sad rather than give up. Read Jesus on the cost, then read what the Lord promises to people who let go. When you read, look for what you get back.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 3, "Endure to the End"
days.journal: King Lamoni's father said "I will give away all my sins to know thee." What's the one thing you'd have a hard time giving away? Write it. Then write what it's actually costing you.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to Mark. Read it once more, especially "Jesus beholding him loved him." Then read what you wrote on Day 1 and Day 4.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: What would Jesus tell you to sell? And are you going to?

question: Why did Jesus flip tables? When is anger right?
intro: Jesus walked into the temple, made a whip, and drove people out. Overturned tables. Coins everywhere. Twice, actually, once at the start of His ministry and once at the end. That's the same Jesus who said turn the other cheek. So either anger is sometimes right, or Jesus was inconsistent. Let's figure out which, because you're going to be angry at something this week, and it'd be good to know if you're allowed.

days.q: What did He do, and what did He say?
days.intro: Read John's account, which is the early one and includes the whip. Then read Matthew's, which is the late one and includes what He quoted. When you read, notice what He's angry *about*. It's specific.
days.journal: What's the last thing that made you truly angry? Write it down. We'll test it this week.

days.q: What was going on in the temple?
days.intro: The moneychangers were in the Court of the Gentiles, the only part of the temple non-Jews were allowed in. It was supposed to be their place to pray. Instead it was a market, and a crooked one. Jesus quotes two scriptures when He clears it out: Isaiah, about the temple being for all nations, and Jeremiah, about a den of robbers. Read both. Then you'll know exactly what He was mad about.
days.journal: When has your behavior kept someone else from getting to God?

days.q: When were Book of Mormon prophets angry?
days.intro: Captain Moroni tore his coat and made a flag. He was angry, and the scriptures call him a man of perfect understanding. Then read the Lord telling Joseph Smith exactly how to be sharp with someone: rarely, with the Spirit, and then with more love afterward. When you read, look for what separates righteous anger from the other kind.
days.journal: D&C 121 says you can reprove with sharpness, but only when moved by the Spirit, and then show more love afterward. When's the last time you did the sharpness part without the love part?

days.q: What does the prophet say about anger?
days.intro: President Russell M. Nelson, April 2023. He gave this talk about contention and it's blunt. Read it next to the table-flipping and see if you can hold both.
days.takeaway: His point is that contention is of the devil, full stop, and that how we treat people who disagree with us is a test of discipleship. He says anger is never the right response to someone being wrong. That sounds like it contradicts Jesus in the temple, until you notice Jesus wasn't contending with anyone. He wasn't in an argument. He was clearing a room so people could pray.
days.journal: Nelson says how you treat people who disagree with you is a test. How'd you do this week?

days.q: So is anger a sin or not?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. 3 Nephi 11 says contention is of the devil. Paul says be angry and sin not. Jesus flipped tables and also said whoever is angry with his brother is in danger. The Joseph Smith Translation removes "without a cause" from that verse. So when is anger right? Read these and find the line. It's there, but it's thin.
days.journal: Go back to what made you angry on Day 1. Was it the temple kind, where someone was blocking access to God? Or the other kind? Be honest.

days.q: How do you get angry the right way?
days.intro: Nephi got angry at his brothers and then called it a weakness he needed to fix. Moroni got angry and built a flag. The difference is what the anger *produced*. Read the Lord's instruction to Joseph about how to handle people who wrong you. When you read, look for what to do with the feeling.
days.journal: Next time you're angry this week, do one thing before you react: ask whether it's about someone getting to God or about you. Write down what happened.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to the temple. Read John once more. Then read your Day 1 and Day 5 answers.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: Why did Jesus flip tables? And when is your anger right?

question: Why do we need another book? What does the Book of Mormon actually do?
intro: Most Christians have the Bible and think that's enough. We show up with a second book and say it's scripture too. Why? What does the Book of Mormon do that the Bible doesn't? If you can't answer that, you're carrying it around out of habit. This week is about what the book is *for*, according to the book itself and according to the prophets who told us to read it.

days.q: Did the Bible say another book was coming?
days.intro: Ezekiel talks about two sticks, Judah's and Joseph's, being joined into one. Isaiah talks about a sealed book that a learned man can't read. Jesus says He has other sheep. Read these cold, without the Sunday School answers, and see what you'd make of them if you'd never heard of the Book of Mormon.
days.journal: Before this week, what would you have said to a friend who asked why you need a second book? Write it.

days.q: What did the Bible lose along the way?
days.intro: Nephi saw it in vision: a book going from the Jews to the Gentiles, and "many plain and precious things" taken out along the way. Not by bad people necessarily, just by time and copying and translation. The Book of Mormon calls itself the fix. Read Nephi's vision, then read what the Lord says about people who claim the Bible is enough.
days.journal: Nephi saw that plain and precious things got lost over time. What's something plain and precious you've lost track of in your own life?

days.q: What does the book say it's for?
days.intro: The title page was written by Moroni, and it states the purpose in one sentence. Read it. Then read the intro and Moroni's promise at the end. When you read, write down every purpose the book claims for itself. There are more than you'd think.
read: Title Page of the Book of Mormon
Introduction to the Book of Mormon (first four paragraphs)
days.journal: The title page says the book exists to convince people that Jesus is the Christ. Has it done that for you, or do you believe in Jesus for other reasons?

days.q: What does the prophet say the book does for you?
days.intro: President Russell M. Nelson, October 2017. He asks a question in the title and then answers it with a list.

read.talk: The Book of Mormon: What Would Your Life Be Like without It?
read.speaker: Russell M. Nelson

days.takeaway: His point is that the book isn't just true, it's *useful*. He lists what it does: it clarifies the Atonement, it teaches how the Holy Ghost works, it exposes the enemies of Christ, it gives you a covenant path. He says something is fundamentally wrong if you'd rather do anything else than read it. And he promises that reading it every day changes you, not just informs you.
days.journal: Nelson asks what your life would be like without it. Answer him. Honestly, what would be different?

days.q: Why not just the Bible?
days.intro: Here's the hard part, and it's the one your friends ask. If the Bible is the word of God, why isn't it sufficient? Isn't adding to it exactly what Revelation warns about? Read the Revelation verse in context. Then read the Lord's argument about two witnesses. Then read a chapter that's only in the Book of Mormon and ask yourself what you'd lose without it.
read: Revelation 22:18-19 (then check Deuteronomy 4:2, same warning, and the Bible kept adding books after it)
2 Nephi 2:22-27 (the Fall explained; the Bible never does this)
days.journal: Pick one thing you believe that comes *only* from the Book of Mormon. Write it down. What would you believe about that topic with just the Bible?

days.q: How do you actually read it?
days.intro: Reading the Book of Mormon front to back is fine, but that's not how it changes you. Nelson's method: read with a question. Look for what it says about Christ. Mark it. Then read Moroni's promise as instructions, not a nice thought: read, remember, ask, with real intent. When you read, figure out what "real intent" means. It's more than sincere.
read: Alma 37:38-46 (the Liahona worked by faith and attention)
Preach My Gospel, lesson 1, "The Book of Mormon: Another Testament of Jesus Christ"
days.journal: Pick one question you want the Book of Mormon to answer. Write it down. Read one chapter tonight looking for it. Write what you found.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to Ezekiel's two sticks. Read it one more time. Then read your Day 1 answer.
days.journal: Answer the week's question the way you'd say it to that friend: Why do we need another book? What does it do?
